title_en: I Have to Go in Chinese

sentences.en: In the evening, I ate dinner at Xiaomei's place, and after dinner, we watched TV together.
After watching for a while, I checked the time and said: "It's getting late, I have to go."
Xiaomei said: "Sit a little longer, it's still early."
I said: "No, I still have to work tomorrow, I'm heading out first."
I stood up and said: "I'm heading out first, bye!"

t: to turn one's head; to look back
sentences.en: I started walking, then looked back — she was still standing at the door.

vocab: to turn one's head; to look back

quiz.q: What does 我要走了 mean?
Why doesn't the writer stay longer at Xiaomei's house?
What does the writer do right before leaving?

grammar.p: 我要走了 / 我先走了（I have to go / I'm heading out first）
grammar.e: Both phrases announce that you're about to leave; 先 adds that you're leaving before others.
grammar.x: 时间不早了，我要走了。— It's getting late, I have to go.

grammar.e: 起来 after a verb like 站 shows upward movement, such as standing up.
grammar.x: 我站了起来，说：“我先走了，再见！”— I stood up and said: "I'm heading out first, bye!"

grammar.e: 回头 describes turning your head to look behind you, often as you're walking away.
grammar.x: 我走了，回头看，她还站在门口。— I started walking, then looked back — she was still standing at the door.
